flags.summary: Internally confirmed that the six-instalment plan totals $7,200 against a $6,000 headline, a 20% uplift that reps disclose to prospects only as 'a bit of interest'.
evidence: So I guess you could frame it like, do you know what the total is with the interest if they take the longest payment plan?
It would end up being, like, $7,200, because it's $1,200 a month.
Okay, great. So that's six for the six months, right?
Well, it kind of is, because there is interest on the payment plans. And the incentive is to go towards the 12-month.

flags.summary: Reps are instructed to withhold the existence of standard payment plans and to tell prospects terms are bespoke, in order to make the financial-disclosure play land.
evidence: I don't want to give any sort of inclination that we can do a payment plan. I don't want them to think we can do that until you open wallet them.
So it always works to hold the payment plans, because then it gives the open wallet validity, because you're saying we don't really have semi-payment plans, it's all custom.
Because until you know financial situation, they're either going to take the lowest payment plan, or you're going to give them the lowest payment plan.
You already told them the lowest thing you could do.

flags.summary: The taught open-wallet worked example prescribes a $1,200 monthly instalment to a prospect who has just disclosed $800 a month of surplus.
evidence: So at the end of each month after you've paid all the bills and everything, how much is usually left over? $800.
And then what about checkings and savings? What do you actually have available right now that you can put towards this that isn't going towards anything else? I have $3,000.
I have $1,000 on one and I have $1,500 on the other.
I think it makes sense for us to do a six pack. I think you do $1,200 today and then just continue on with $1,200 a month. That seems like it'd be feasible for you.

flags.summary: Reps are coached to recommend that prospects put the purchase on a credit card, framed as proof of commitment.
evidence: they'll be like, dude, I have a credit card with like $20,000 on it. I'd like, oh, can I tell you what I would do if I were you? And be like, what? Like, dude, I would put it on the credit card. Here's why. Number one, you're all in.
And that's what most people do. They just put it on a credit card and so it gives them the flexibility. It also means that you're 100% all in.
So why don't we just do that, bro? And then what's going to come up? Fear. That's it. So then I just handle fear.
I've gotten more pissed from open wallets than I've ever done just offering payment plans.

flags.summary: A prospect's disclosed pain is reviewed by rep and manager solely as a missed discovery opportunity, with no mention of medical screening or clearance.
evidence: he came on saying that... one of things I want to work on is my posture. I'm tight. I have muscle pain.
I feel like I could have actually probed deeper into like, when you say pain, like, where do you feel the pain? How often do you feel it? Like, scale one to 10, 10 being the highest?
He mentioned he wants to, he has some back pain and joint pain. And he mentioned he wants to like, you know, keep up with his kids and cares about longevity
Yeah, you can definitely challenge somebody like that.

flags.summary: The manager's tier-recommendation heuristic is built around prospects with 40 to 50 pounds to lose, a population the stated ICP explicitly excludes.
evidence: If I find out through their situation that they need the 12, I tell them the 12.
If they have a lot more weight to lose, like they have to lose like 40, 50 pounds, then yeah, I'd probably tell them the 12. If they need to lose like 20 pounds, I'd tell them the six.
that's probably what you're dealing with is you're getting a lot of these people that like they already have been taking their health decently seriously. They just need to get to the next level.
